content: 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends improving access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene services to reduce the incidence of infections and enhance nutritional outcomes. This includes promoting preventive chemotherapy, such as the periodic large-scale administration of anthelmintic medications, to significantly reduce the burden of soil-transmitted helminth infections. 2. Preventive chemotherapy (deworming) using single-dose albendazole (400 mg) or mebendazole (500 mg) annually or biannually is recommended as a public health intervention for young children (12–23 months), preschool children (24–59 months), and school-age children living in areas where the baseline prevalence of soil-transmitted helminth infections is 20% or higher among children. This intervention aims to reduce the worm burden caused by these infections. 3. Preventive chemotherapy (deworming) is also recommended for non-pregnant adolescent girls (10–19 years) and non-pregnant women of reproductive age (15–49 years) in areas where the baseline prevalence of soil-transmitted helminth infections is 20% or higher among these groups. The goal is to reduce the worm burden in these populations. 4. Pregnant women, after the first trimester, living in areas where the prevalence of hookworm and/or Trichuris trichiura infections is 20% or higher and where anemia is a severe public health problem (prevalence of 40% or higher among pregnant women), should also receive preventive chemotherapy with single-dose albendazole (400 mg) or mebendazole (500 mg). This intervention aims to reduce the worm burden and associated health risks. 5. Access to safe, separate, and private sanitation facilities is essential for menstrual hygiene management, dignity, comfort, and health among adolescent girls. Reliable facilities at home, schools, workplaces, and within communities enable girls to engage in daily routines without constraints. 6. Inadequate school sanitation facilities contribute to irregular school attendance and increase the likelihood of dropping out, which can make adolescent girls more vulnerable to early marriage and early childbearing. 7. Children are more susceptible to environmental diseases than adults. Low-cost interventions to improve the physical environment in schools, such as ensuring clean and safe drinking water, proper waste disposal, and safe food services, can significantly enhance children’s health and nutrition. 8. Promoting physical activity among adolescents is critical for their musculoskeletal development, bone health, cardiovascular fitness, and neuromuscular awareness. It also helps reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression, supports energy balance, and prevents obesity. 9. Adolescents should engage in at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity daily. Activities exceeding 60 minutes provide additional health benefits. Most of this activity should be aerobic, with vigorous-intensity activities, including muscleand bone-strengthening exercises, incorporated at least three times per week. 10. For adults aged 18–64 years, at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity per week is recommended. Additional health benefits can be achieved by increasing moderate-intensity activity to 300 minutes per week or engaging in 150 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity weekly. Muscle-strengthening activities involving major muscle groups should be performed on two or more days per week. 11. Policymakers should ensure the availability of school and public spaces for physical activity and develop multicomponent programs to promote structured sports and physical activity in schools, communities, and workplaces. Public awareness campaigns on the importance of physical activity should also be implemented. 12. Tailored interventions to promote physical activity among adolescents should consider cultural contexts, gender issues, and disease burdens specific to each country. This approach ensures that recommended levels of physical activity are achieved. 13. Research gaps exist in addressing adolescent nutrition, particularly in understanding the coexistence of undernutrition with overweight, obesity, or risk factors for diet-related non-communicable diseases. Further research is needed to assess dietary patterns, behavioral profiles, and the main influencers of adolescents to inform programs and policies. 14. Health services for adolescents are often fragmented, poorly coordinated, and uneven in quality. Adolescents frequently find mainstream primary care services unacceptable due to perceived lack of respect, privacy, and confidentiality, as well as fear of stigma and discrimination. 15. WHO has developed global standards for quality care in adolescent health services, emphasizing the need for respectful, confidential, and equitable care that actively involves adolescents in decision-making processes.
